content: In the IMPAACT P1060 study, 81% of children who initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) based on lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) achieved viral suppression to less than 50 copies/mL within six months, compared to only 59% of those on nevirapine (NVP)-based ART. Early viral load suppression was significantly lower in individuals with baseline viral loads exceeding 100,000 copies/mL, even among those receiving dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens. Similarly, children with viral loads above 100,000 copies/mL demonstrated poor suppression rates at one and three months after starting ART. Detecting treatment failure due to pretreatment drug resistance earlier would be advantageous, particularly for individuals on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens. However, it is critical to balance this with the risk of overestimating treatment failure if viral load testing is conducted too early, which could lead to unnecessary therapy switches. The 2016 treatment monitoring algorithm recommends the first viral load test be performed six months after initiating ART. However, evidence shows that for many people living with HIV, sample collection, testing, and result delivery often occur beyond this timeframe. The updated algorithm emphasizes the need for the first viral load result to be urgently available and reviewed within six months of ART initiation. The current viral load algorithm suggests a second viral load test 3–6 months after an initial elevated result (>1,000 copies/mL). However, literature reviews indicate that this timeframe lacks clarity, leading to inconsistent implementation and substantial delays in repeat testing. Factors contributing to these delays include issues with specimen transport, laboratory testing, result delivery, and patient return for counseling or repeat testing. A more precise timeframe for repeat viral load testing could improve consistency and adherence while emphasizing the importance of timely testing. Conducting a repeat viral load test earlier than six months could reduce the accumulation of drug resistance, particularly for those on NNRTI-based regimens, and minimize onward transmission. However, testing one month after an elevated viral load result may overestimate treatment failure, leading to unnecessary treatment switches when adherence interventions might suffice. A three-month interval for repeat testing may allow for more rapid clinical action, preventing further drug resistance and transmission of resistant virus. Switching ART regimens immediately after a single elevated viral load result is only considered for NNRTI-based regimens, not for DTGor protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimens, as resistance to NNRTIs is high in lowand middle-income countries. National surveys of acquired drug resistance among adults with a single elevated viral load result showed NNRTI resistance prevalence ranging from 50% in Eswatini to 97% in Uganda at 12 months after ART initiation. Resistance rates ranged from 71% in Nicaragua to 92% in Senegal 48 months or later after starting ART. Studies of adults on tenofovir (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) + efavirenz (EFV) regimens in lowand middle-income countries reported NNRTI mutation prevalence at failure ranging from 42% in eastern Africa to 82% in western and central Africa, with southern Africa at 59%. Children and adolescents on NNRTI-based regimens also exhibit high levels of drug resistance. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that 46% of individuals on NNRTI-based first-line ART with elevated viral loads resuppressed at the next viral load test, suggesting poor adherence in many cases. Resuppression rates were lower among children (31%) and adolescents (40%) compared to adults (50%). Surveys of values and preferences among adolescents and adults living with HIV indicate a preference for allowing time to achieve viral load suppression. Cost-effectiveness modeling suggests that switching adults from NNRTI-based ART to second-line ART after a single elevated viral load result (>1,000 copies/mL) has health benefits, reduces HIV transmission and mortality, and is cost-effective, particularly for those with drug resistance. Switching after a single elevated viral load result is cost-effective at a threshold of US$500 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. Evidence suggests that 40–97% of individuals in lowand middle-income countries on NNRTI-based ART with a single elevated viral load have drug resistance and would benefit from immediate switching to second-line ART. Despite WHO recommendations, fewer than 25% of individuals with an initial elevated viral load complete the viral load cascade (adherence counseling and repeat testing). Faster ART switching for those on NNRTI-based regimens would reduce the risk of further drug resistance and onward transmission, which is especially critical for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Clinical support is necessary to ensure timely switching to second-line ART. However, some individuals with high viral loads may face adherence challenges, requiring support to address these issues. Emphasizing adherence during ART initiation and throughout treatment is essential, including enhanced counseling for those with elevated viral load results. The Guideline Development Group determined that while some individuals on NNRTI-based regimens may not have drug resistance and could be unnecessarily switched to second-line ART, switching after a single elevated viral load result would yield significant personal and public health benefits. Immediate ART switching after a single elevated viral load result should not be considered for those on DTGor PI-based regimens, as the likelihood of drug resistance is minimal based on current evidence. A review of 31 studies on low-level viremia (LLV) among adults on ART found a prevalence ranging from 3% to 26%, with LLV generally defined as one or more viral load results between 50 and 1,000 copies/mL. LLV was associated with future virological failure, defined as viral load >500 or >1,000 copies/mL after a period of LLV. Viral loads between 50 and 200 copies/mL tended to predict future failure, while those between 200 and 500 copies/mL significantly predicted failure. Eight cohort studies examined the development of drug resistance mutations during LLV episodes, finding that detectable viral loads under 1,000 copies/mL were associated with new resistance mutations. No studies assessed these outcomes for individuals on DTG, and the clinical relevance of LLV for those on DTGor PI-based regimens remains unclear. Seven studies on HIV transmission during LLV episodes found no evidence of transmission within adult couples when the HIV-positive partner had viral loads under 200 copies/mL, and one study found no transmission events with viral loads under 1,500 copies/mL. LLV (<1,000 copies/mL) was not associated with sexual transmission. A review updating the Spectrum mathematical model summarized the risk of vertical transmission by maternal viral load, with low transmission rates observed even at low viral loads. No studies evaluated HIV transmissibility through shared injecting drug use equipment at viral loads under 1,000 copies/mL. Implementation considerations for the treatment monitoring algorithm include the use of dried blood spots, point-of-care technologies, or alternative specimen types to expand access to viral load testing. Some technologies perform reliably at lower treatment failure thresholds, while others show poor sensitivity and specificity. Additional studies are needed to better understand performance. Experts emphasized the importance of distinguishing viral suppression or undetectable virus from treatment failure requiring therapy switching. The transition to DTG-based regimens across countries should also be recognized. The Guideline Development Group recommended maintaining the treatment failure threshold at 1,000 copies/mL. Strengthening adherence counseling during ART initiation and throughout treatment is essential, particularly after elevated viral load results. Viral load results can motivate adherence and achieving viral suppression. Adequate training on ART for clinicians, healthcare providers, and peer counselors is necessary, including guidance on optimal regimens, treatment failure, therapy switching, and adherence support. Testing pregnant and breastfeeding women with point-of-care technologies enables rapid clinical decision-making to prevent transmission. Drug resistance rates are higher among infants, children, and adolescents than adults, and rapid results can prevent the selection of resistance mutations, preserving future treatment options. Treatment failure thresholds should not be equated with being undetectable or suppressed. All individuals living with HIV should receive adherence counseling to achieve viral suppression, but treatment failure should be considered for those with repeat viral load results >1,000 copies/mL three months after an initial elevated result.
